title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
text:
ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-19
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved this decision and the nine decisions of the device enrollment and lifecycle design on 2026-10-19 under PH-22. Acceptance establishes the direction for local and CI implementation of PJ-08 with simulated players, not Android player delivery (PJ-12), hardware qualification (PH-08) or production readiness.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Context
text:
Context
Teluni screens are Android TV players without a keyboard that must be paired to one company and branch by a person who is already signed in to the panel (FR-02). Policies require temporary, single-use, rate-limited codes that are safe under concurrent claims, a separate revocable identity per device that is never a human principal, revocation that denies future server access, and no custom cryptography or token schemes ([security requirements](../project/security-and-i18n.md#pairing-and-device-lifecycle), [release policies](../project/release-policies.md#offline-authorization-and-clock-trust)). Keycloak holds only human identities ([ADR-0024](0024-propose-keycloak-and-server-managed-human-sessions.md)), and the pilot runs on a single host ([ADR-0021](0021-propose-a-single-host-pilot-with-portable-persistent-storage.md)).
This record decides how a device is enrolled and how it authenticates afterward. The detailed rules, limits, data and contracts are in the [device enrollment and lifecycle design](../project/device-enrollment-design.md).

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Teluni will enroll devices with an application-owned flow shaped like the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628) and authenticate them with a device-generated bearer credential:
The player generates a 256-bit credential from the platform CSPRNG, keeps it in Android Keystore-backed storage and sends only its SHA-256 when it starts an enrollment. The API answers with a short user code to display and an enrollment ID to poll.
A signed-in, authorized person enters the user code in the panel; one conditional transaction claims the enrollment and creates the device in the chosen company and branch.
The device then presents the credential as a bearer token on device routes only. The API stores only the hash, resolves it on every request without caching, and revokes it by state change. Human routes never accept it and device routes never accept a human session.
User codes are short-lived, single-use, stored only as a keyed HMAC and protected by attempt limits.
The API's devices module owns the flow; the shared runtime gains only a `device` operation access kind. No identity provider, certificate authority or proof-of-possession library is introduced now.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
RFC 8628 is the established pattern for input-constrained devices, so the user-facing shape and its code guidance (alphabet, length, expiry, rate limits) come from a reviewed standard rather than invention. Generating the credential on the device means no secret is ever returned by the server, so a lost response at any step is retried without issuing anything and without a re-issue path. A 256-bit random value needs only a plain hash for storage and lookup. A bearer credential over HTTPS fits the single-host pilot and the existing Fastify/PostgreSQL stack.
The accepted cost is that a copied credential is usable until revoked, unlike a key that never leaves hardware. Revocation on the next request, rotation and the `device` access kind as a single seam keep a later move to proof of possession contained.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Server-issued credential returned at pairing
text:
Server-issued credential returned at pairing
Returning the only copy of a secret in one response makes a lost response either a stuck device or a reason to add a re-issue path with more secret-bearing responses.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Device key pair with signed requests or mutual TLS
text:
Device key pair with signed requests or mutual TLS
DPoP (RFC 9449) or client certificates would keep the private key in hardware and resist copying. They add proof verification or certificate issuance and renewal without a measured threat that requires them in the pilot. They remain the preferred upgrade if PH-08 devices offer usable hardware-backed keys and the threat model calls for it.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Keycloak device grant and service accounts
text:
Keycloak device grant and service accounts
It reuses an established server, but makes each screen a Keycloak client or user, couples player operation to Keycloak availability and mixes device and human identities that the policies keep apart.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
No secret leaves the server, and every enrollment step is safely retryable.
Revocation is immediate for reachable devices and needs no token lists or expiry windows.
Device and human authentication stay separate at the operation level.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
A credential copied from a compromised or rooted device works until revoked; physical control of a player remains a residual risk, as the security requirements already state.
Teluni owns the enrollment endpoints, limits and their tests instead of relying on an identity provider.
A new `RESTRICTED` key ring for user-code HMACs must be configured and rotated.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Host migration and restore must preserve credential hashes so devices keep working, without ever exporting the credentials themselves.
Moving to proof of possession later requires a player update and an overlap period in which both schemes are accepted for already-paired devices.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
text:
ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-19
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved this decision and the nine decisions of the media library design on 2026-10-19 under PH-23. Acceptance establishes the direction for local and CI implementation of PJ-09 with generated fixtures, not device profile qualification (PH-08), the production image (PJ-13) or malware scanning (PH-13).

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Context
text:
Context
Teluni stores private customer images and videos, validates them against the selected ingestion bounds and turns them into renditions that Android TV screens can play offline (FR-04, AT-02, AT-03). The pilot runs on one residential host with durable mounted storage and no cloud budget, and media storage must stay a media-owned capability with replaceable filesystem I/O ([ADR-0021](0021-propose-a-single-host-pilot-with-portable-persistent-storage.md)). Security requirements ask for trustworthy inspection, parser isolation and no unvalidated transcoding framework ([security requirements](../project/security-and-i18n.md#media-and-audit-protections)); the release policies require preserved originals, compatible renditions, reference-safe deletion and a recoverable trash.
This record decides where media bytes live, how they are named and published, and which tool parses and converts untrusted files, and how it is isolated. The detailed rules, profiles, limits, data and contracts are in the [media library design](../project/media-library-design.md).

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Teluni will store media as immutable content-addressed objects on a local volume and process it only with FFmpeg in isolated child processes:
The media module owns an object interface (`put`, `open` with an optional byte range, `delete`, `list`) implemented over a configured directory on durable storage. Each object is named by the SHA-256 of its bytes inside its company and is never modified; identical bytes are stored once per company and never shared across companies.
Objects are written to a work directory on the same filesystem, flushed, and published by an atomic rename while a transaction-scoped PostgreSQL advisory lock on the object is held, before the referencing asset commits. PostgreSQL is the authority for which objects exist and who may read them; paths never leave the module.
Untrusted files are parsed and converted only by the FFmpeg executables (`ffprobe`, `ffmpeg`, version 6.1 or later), run without a shell, with a scrubbed environment, a forced demuxer, the file protocol only, bounded output and timeouts, and resource limits where the host offers them. No media parser or image library runs inside the API process.
Work is queued in PostgreSQL and claimed by an in-process processor with leases, so several API processes can share it and interrupted work resumes.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Content addressing makes objects immutable, integrity checkable and deduplicated, which publications (ADR-0019) need for manifests and the player's shared-file accounting (AT-05). Publishing by rename under the object lock gives a simple crash rule: a file may exist without a reference and is swept, but a reference never exists without its file. Per-company naming keeps tenants independent at the cost of storing a file twice when two companies upload it.
FFmpeg is the established tool for both inspection and conversion of every format the release needs, including EXIF orientation and metadata removal for images, so one external tool covers both kinds instead of FFmpeg plus an in-process image library. Running it as a separate executable keeps memory-safety defects in parsers out of the API process and lets timeouts and limits kill a hostile file. It also keeps Teluni's Apache-2.0 code separate from FFmpeg's GPL build. The trade-off is CPU-heavy work on the API host and a binary dependency that every environment must provide.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: S3-compatible object storage now
text:
S3-compatible object storage now
A MinIO or cloud bucket would separate storage from the API host and scale later, but it adds a service to run on the single-host pilot or a paid dependency. The object interface keeps this as a later implementation without changing object identity.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Media in PostgreSQL
text:
Media in PostgreSQL
Large objects or `bytea` would make storage transactional, but they inflate database backups and I/O with gigabytes of video and complicate streaming and range reads.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: libvips (sharp) for images and FFmpeg for video
text:
libvips (`sharp`) for images and FFmpeg for video
Faster image handling, but it parses untrusted images inside the API process and adds a second native toolchain to qualify and isolate.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: A separate processing service with a broker
text:
A separate processing service with a broker
Stronger isolation and independent scaling, but it adds deployment and failure modes that the pilot does not yet need. A separate, network-less processing container running the same commands is the deployment-level hardening step, without changing this decision.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Immutable, verifiable objects that publications and players can reference by hash.
Crash-safe publication and reference-safe purge with a single lock order.
Hostile files cannot run code in, or exhaust, the API process.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Conversion competes with the API for CPU on the pilot host; concurrency is limited to one job by default and long videos take minutes.
Every environment (development, CI, production image) must provide a compatible FFmpeg build, and its security updates become an operational duty.
Storage is tied to one host until another object store implementation exists; backups must cover the media volume together with PostgreSQL.

title: ADR-0028: Adopt Local Content-Addressed Media Storage and Isolated FFmpeg Processing
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Backups and restore must copy the media volume and the database consistently; restored objects are verified against their hashes, and a sweep removes files without rows.
Moving to another object store copies objects by hash and switches the implementation; asset and object identities stay the same.
The production image must ship FFmpeg with its license notices (PJ-13).

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
text:
ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
**Status:** proposed
**Date:** 2026-10-19

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Context
text:
Context
Teluni schedules playlists by local business time per screen: weekdays, local hours, overnight windows, inclusive final dates and all-day windows, interpreted in the screen's time zone or its branch's, never the server's (FR-06). The [release policies](../project/release-policies.md#time-and-scheduling) fix how DST gaps and repeated hours resolve and require the backend preview and the Android player to share fixtures. Node.js 24, the API runtime, does not ship the ECMAScript Temporal API, and the standard `Date` and `Intl` objects give offsets for an instant but no way to resolve a local time that falls in a gap or a repeated hour. D-10 has not selected a time-zone library.
This record decides how the API represents and resolves local time for schedules and how the API and the player agree on the results. The rules themselves are in the [programming design](../project/programming-design.md).

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Teluni will evaluate schedules with a pure evaluator over the Temporal API and verify every implementation against one fixture file:
The API's programming module owns a pure TypeScript evaluator that takes rules, a default, an IANA zone name and an instant range and returns resolved segments. It never reads a clock or the process time zone.
Local dates and times are Temporal `PlainDate` and `PlainTime` values, instants are Temporal `Instant` values, and zone resolution uses `ZonedDateTime` with explicit disambiguation plus transition lookup for gaps. Until Node.js provides Temporal natively, the API uses the `temporal-polyfill` package, pinned to an exact version, imported only by the programming module.
Canonical fixtures in JSON (rules, zone, range and expected segments in UTC and local form, and expected validation codes) are owned by the API module and run by its tests. The player runs the same file against its implementation in PJ-12; neither implementation is the reference for the other.
Preview is computed only by the API; the panel displays its segments.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Temporal models exactly the concepts the policies use (plain local dates and times, instants, zones and explicit disambiguation), and its model matches `java.time`, which an Android player is expected to use, so both implementations reason in the same terms and the fixtures express the same cases. A spec-conformant polyfill keeps the code on the standard API, so removing it when Node.js ships Temporal is an import change rather than a rewrite. Fixtures, not shared code, are the contract between two runtimes in different languages. Keeping the evaluator pure makes validation, preview and tests deterministic and independent of the host.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Luxon or date-fns-tz
text:
Luxon or date-fns-tz
Mature libraries, but each has its own model of gaps and repeated hours that differs from `java.time` and from the standard on the way to Node.js, so the fixtures would encode library behavior rather than the policy.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Hand-written resolution over Intl.DateTimeFormat
text:
Hand-written resolution over `Intl.DateTimeFormat`
Avoids a dependency, but searching transitions and disambiguating local times is where subtle errors appear, and the code would duplicate a standard that is about to ship.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: A shared evaluator package compiled for both runtimes
text:
A shared evaluator package compiled for both runtimes
One implementation for the API and the player would remove the second implementation, but the player is a native Android application; embedding a JavaScript engine to run schedules adds a runtime and its own failure modes on the device.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Deterministic, host-independent schedule results with the selected DST rules.
One fixture file that both the API and the player must pass.
A direct path to native Temporal.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
A runtime dependency in the API until Node.js ships Temporal, which must be kept current with the zone database it relies on (the polyfill uses the runtime's `Intl` zone data).
Two implementations of the evaluator, kept equal only by the fixtures.

title: ADR-0029: Evaluate Schedules with the Temporal API and Shared Fixtures
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Zone data comes from the Node.js runtime's ICU; updating Node.js updates zone rules, and preview results for future dates can change after a zone-database update, as on the device.
Replacing the polyfill with native Temporal removes the dependency and its import; the fixtures must still pass.

title: ADR Instructions
heading: ADR Instructions
text:
ADR Instructions
Consult the [decision index](README.md) and [authoring policy](authoring.md) before creating or changing an ADR.
Start new proposals with the [template](template.md) and `proposed` status. Acceptance is distinct from implementation completion.
Preserve accepted rationale, decisions, dates, and stable identifiers. Architectural changes require a new decision and explicit supersession, not rewritten history.
Retain meaningful alternatives, negative consequences, constraints, and evidence. Do not invent evaluations to fill the template.
Update current policy and reciprocal supersession references when an accepted architectural change requires them.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
text:
Authoring Architecture Decision Records
Use the [decision index](README.md) to search existing decisions and the [template](template.md) to draft a record. ADRs preserve decision history and rationale; current policy describes current architecture. Git, migrations, changelogs, design documents, and runbooks retain their separate responsibilities.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: When a decision needs an ADR
text:
When a decision needs an ADR
Create an ADR for a significant choice whose rationale a future contributor cannot reliably infer from implementation. Relevant effects include system boundaries, dependency direction, ownership, runtime/deployment topology, security, persistence, public contracts, cross-cutting technology, operational behavior, and long-term maintainability.
Consider the breadth, reversibility, long-term dependency, plausible alternatives, integrity/security implications, and risk of losing the reasoning. Ordinary local refactors, fixes, tests, small helpers, individual indexes, and routine dependency additions do not each need an ADR. Major technology choices generally do. Existing foundation policies do not each need retroactive ADRs.
An ADR records a sufficiently concrete architectural conclusion, not every discussion or rejected idea. It must not become a task tracker, changelog, runbook, detailed implementation design, or snapshot of volatile vendor data. A separate RFC system is not required. Bundle decisions only when their rationale and lifecycle belong together; avoid giant records deciding unrelated parts of the stack.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Lifecycle and historical integrity
text:
Lifecycle and historical integrity
Status
Meaning
`proposed`
Under active consideration; implementation must not assume finality unless explicitly exploratory
`accepted`
Approved architectural direction; implementation and current documentation should align, allowing an explicit migration period
`rejected`
Considered and deliberately not adopted
`superseded`
Previously accepted, then replaced by another decision; link the replacement
`deprecated`
Historically relevant but no longer appropriate for new architecture; use sparingly when replacement is transitional or incomplete
Do not add statuses without a clear need. Normal transitions are proposed to accepted/rejected and accepted to superseded/deprecated. Do not normally revert historical decisions to proposed; create a new record when reconsidering them.
Accepted does not mean implemented or released. Track pending/partial/completed implementation through normal issues, tasks, or pull requests, not extra ADR statuses. Exploratory work and proofs of concept provide evidence but do not themselves establish acceptance. Long-lived production implementation should generally not rely on an unresolved major proposal.
Accepted substantive history should remain immutable. Non-semantic spelling, formatting, broken-link, and obvious-typo corrections may be acceptable, but must not change historical meaning. When architecture changes, create a new ADR. Retain the old record, mark it superseded, and add reciprocal `Supersedes` / `Superseded by` references. Keep the original date. For partial supersession, identify precisely what remains valid, what changed, and which decision replaces it.
Rejected records can preserve useful evaluation and constraints; a changed context can justify reconsideration in a new ADR. Do not treat rejection as a permanent prohibition. Purely local abandoned proposals may be removed before meaningful shared history; preserve broadly reviewed or referenced proposals as rejected where useful. Do not record every immediately dismissed idea.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Identity and metadata
text:
Identity and metadata
Use monotonic numeric identifiers and descriptive English filenames of the form `NNNN-short-decision-title.md`. Numbers identify records, not importance, domain, priority, or version. Gaps are acceptable. Never reuse or renumber identifiers already in shared history. Resolve parallel numbering conflicts before merge; an unshared identifier may be changed.
Record title, status, date, context, decision, and consequences. For accepted records, the date should generally be the acceptance date. Titles should describe the decision rather than merely name a topic. Preserve identifiers once merged and referenced.
Simple Markdown metadata is the current format. `pnpm docs:check` validates filenames, matching titles/IDs, status, ISO dates, required sections, and index membership. Preserve these field names as tooling contracts. Supersession semantics still require review; no automatic numbering or supersession checker is implemented. ADR files remain canonical; avoid duplicate status stores or custom ADR software without a concrete need.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Content and evidence
text:
Content and evidence
**Context:** explain the actual problem, relevant constraints, scope, timing, and assumptions. Avoid unnecessary implementation detail.
**Decision:** state the chosen direction clearly enough to understand independently of the alternatives.
**Rationale:** explain the material tradeoffs, evidence, and constraints. Distinguish confirmed evidence, reasoned tradeoffs, and assumptions.
**Alternatives:** describe serious alternatives considered; do not fabricate alternatives or evaluation evidence to fill a template.
**Consequences:** include benefits, costs, limitations, new responsibilities, security/operational effects, and reversibility or migration costs where relevant. Formal scoring is not required.
**References:** link relevant repository policy, earlier decisions, designs, benchmarks, proofs of concept, and durable evidence. Avoid unnecessary dependency graphs and large volatile datasets. Preserve enough explanation that disappearing external links do not destroy the rationale.
Use current evidence at decision time when product capability, support lifecycle, pricing, security status, or provider limits matter. Vendor documentation can support constraints but must not be the sole location of the explanation. Detailed implementation and operational migration steps normally belong outside the ADR.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Creation, review, and acceptance
text:
Creation, review, and acceptance
Search the index and related policies for the same question, accepted direction, superseded decision, or rejected alternative. Determine whether this is an architectural decision rather than an implementation detail.
Allocate the next available identifier, copy the template, and use `proposed` status.
Document context, explicit direction, meaningful alternatives, rationale, constraints, and positive and negative consequences while the context is still known.
Review in proportion to impact: is the problem real, the complexity justified, and the choice consistent with existing architecture? Identify conflicts and intentional deviations explicitly.
Accept or reject through repository review. For a small team, review, merge, and accepted status are sufficient; do not add governance ceremony without a concrete need.
On acceptance, update affected current documentation and implement the selected direction with relevant verification. Do not retain rejected experimental paths unnecessarily.
For supersession, additionally identify changed constraints, reciprocal references, affected current policy, and compatibility/migration work. For rejection, record decisive reasons, preferred alternatives where applicable, and conditions that could justify reconsideration.
Retrospective ADRs should say the decision was already in effect. Record only known reasoning and state uncertainty rather than inventing a historical evaluation. Significant principle deviations belong in the decision and corresponding current-policy update. When later accepted decisions supersede older records, follow the replacement and current policy rather than treating the superseded record as current architecture.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Maintenance and deferred mechanisms
text:
Maintenance and deferred mechanisms
Routine maintenance should be limited to permitted corrections and supersession metadata. Current architecture must remain discoverable without reading the entire chronological ADR history. Keep descriptive titles, explicit technologies/concepts, and useful related references.
Frontmatter, automatic numbering, generated indexing, status/supersession validation, approval workflows, and required reviewers remain tooling or organizational decisions. Introduce them only when justified. ADRs should preserve meaningful reasoning without becoming bureaucratic records for every change.

title: Architecture Decision Records
heading: Architecture Decision Records
text:
Architecture Decision Records
Use this index to locate governing decisions without reading the full history. Each linked record owns its status, decision, rationale, and consequences. Acceptance does not imply implementation; see [validation availability](../validation.md) and the [technology map](../architecture/technology-decisions.md).
For a new decision, read [authoring policy](authoring.md), inspect related records, and use the [proposed template](template.md). Current behavior belongs in the [policy index](../README.md), not in rewritten historical ADRs.

title: API Error Contract
heading: API Error Contract
text:
API Error Contract
[Task index](../README.md) · [API principles](principles.md) · [Error handling](../architecture/error-handling.md) · [Compatibility](versioning.md)
This policy owns public failure semantics. The API's [shared error registry, envelope schema, and responder](../../apps/api/src/errors.ts) and each composed module's registered codes are canonical; the [public registry composition](../../apps/api/src/error-registry.ts) gives each code exactly one owner and rejects any duplicate, even an identical definition, and the [generated error reference](../generated/api/errors.md) lists implemented codes, messages, categories, HTTP statuses, and retry classifications. Module route contracts declare expected operation errors. Follow [ADR-0007](../adr/0007-establish-api-contract-openapi-sdk-and-configuration-schema-strategy.md) when generating OpenAPI and SDK representations.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Error Envelope

title: API Error Contract
heading: Error Code Format
text:
Error Code Format
Public codes use stable semantic `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` names. Clients branch on codes and deliberately defined structured fields, never on message text or internal exception classes. Messages are safe human explanations and may change for clarity or product localization without changing the code's meaning. Canonical repository descriptions remain English.
Infrastructure identifiers such as SQLSTATE, ORM codes, provider exceptions, filesystem paths, or runtime class names are not public semantics. Map failures to the condition consumers need to understand. Reuse an existing code for the same meaning; do not create a code for every code path, collapse materially different consumer actions into one generic code, or reuse a retired code for a new meaning.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Error Code Ownership
text:
Error Code Ownership
The feature/application owner defines business failures; the API boundary owns cross-cutting public mappings. The registry provides one canonical definition, and operation metadata refers to it. The registry enumerates stable public conditions, not every possible database/network/library exception. Do not maintain an independent manual registry in prose or generated clients.
For a new code, determine its semantic owner, expected/unexpected category, public disclosure safety, consumer action, status mapping, retry implications, optional details, and compatibility impact. Update canonical code, operation declarations, tests, and generated references together. Each module's implementation conventions explain its authorization-sensitive classification order.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Validation Errors
text:
Validation Errors
The implemented validation response is `400 VALIDATION_FAILED` with the common envelope. Do not expose validator exceptions or echo submitted values. Structural validation is distinct from a valid request that conflicts with current domain state.
If field-level details become useful, add an explicit bounded schema to the canonical contract. Identify fields using a stable public request-path convention, never internal database/ORM paths; use stable reason codes where clients need to act and safe human text for explanation. Define multiple-failure bounds and unknown-field behavior. Returning every issue in an attacker-controlled payload must not create an unbounded response.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Mapping and disclosure
text:
Mapping and disclosure
HTTP status conveys broad protocol meaning; public codes convey application semantics. The [generated registry](../generated/api/errors.md) is the current status mapping. Validation uses `400`, authentication `401`, permission denial `403`, absent/hidden resources `404`, state/version conflicts `409`, rate limiting `429`, unexpected failures `500`, and service unavailability `503` where declared.
Authentication and authorization failures follow their [security policies](../security/authentication.md). Avoid account enumeration and disclosure of hidden resource existence, cross-tenant data, claims, or policy internals. An absent and inaccessible resource may deliberately share `404`; test that behavior.
Expected domain conflicts, stale versions, and incompatible idempotency-key reuse are explicit outcomes. Distinguish safe replay from a conflicting new intent. They should not become internal incidents simply because code represents them as exceptions.
Translate known database constraints at the persistence/application boundary according to business meaning. Unexpected database failures stay unexpected; do not disguise every exception as invalid user input.
Translate provider business rejection separately from dependency unavailability, configuration failure, or unknown outcome. Expose vendor-specific distinctions only when consumers need them, never raw provider content.
Use a safe generic error for unexpected failures. Never serialize arbitrary exceptions, stack traces, SQL, secret values, internal paths/hostnames, or diagnostic dumps. Do not return ordinary API failures as hidden error objects inside `200` responses.
Public status is not internal severity: expected denials may matter to security monitoring, and a transient dependency failure may be operationally serious. [Error reporting](../reliability/error-reporting.md) owns that distinction.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Unknown Outcome
text:
Unknown Outcome
A timeout, disconnect, or commit error may leave the caller uncertain whether a write or external effect occurred. Retryability cannot be inferred from HTTP status or transient infrastructure failure alone. Define whether the operation is known not to have occurred, safely replayable, or requires state reconciliation. Introduce a distinct public unknown-outcome code only when consumers need different handling.
A public retry hint, if introduced, must be machine-readable, bounded, and accurate for the operation. Rate-limit guidance must not disclose anti-abuse internals. Never imply a non-idempotent write is safe to repeat merely because the registry classifies a failure as transient. Each module's recovery conventions own its create replay and mutation reconciliation behavior.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Details and additional delivery modes
text:
Details and additional delivery modes
Every public details object needs a typed schema and a consumer purpose. Include only information safe for that caller; omit record dumps, protected resource/tenant identifiers, authorization evaluation, credentials, and provider payloads. Cross-cutting correlation/retry metadata should remain distinguishable from domain details. Once consumed, field meaning and shape are compatibility-sensitive.
When additional modes are introduced:
Mode
Error requirement
Webhook or upload
Follow the operation/provider contract while minimizing signature-validation or scanning details. Bound and classify upload failures explicitly.
Asynchronous work
A successful acceptance response does not guarantee eventual success. Externally visible job status maps worker failures to stable public semantics, never worker exceptions.
Batch/partial success
Define atomic versus partial processing and item identity in an operation-specific result. Do not ambiguously overload the ordinary single-error envelope.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Diagnostics and consumer behavior
text:
Diagnostics and consumer behavior
Report an unexpected occurrence once at its authoritative boundary. Preserve useful internal causal evidence only within [redaction rules](../security/telemetry-redaction.md); preservation never authorizes raw exception-message or stack export. The current runtime records allowlisted diagnostic fields rather than arbitrary error content. Expected validation, business, and access failures may contribute to safe metrics/security/audit signals without becoming unexpected incidents.
Clients and SDKs must preserve structured error semantics and correlation, and provide a safe fallback for unknown codes. Application consumers should not depend on framework-specific transport exceptions for business meaning. Product code decides whether to display safe server copy or localized client text; it must not parse that copy. The current thin SDK exposes generated response/error typing without adding a separate error-class hierarchy.
Code meaning, status mappings, details, categories where consumed, and retry behavior require [compatibility review](versioning.md). Adding a code can break exhaustive consumers; renaming/removing a code or changing meaning is potentially breaking. Optional details are only additive if actual clients tolerate them.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Change and verification checklist
text:
Change and verification checklist
Inspect the registry, similar conditions, owning operation, actual consumers, authorization/disclosure policy, and compatibility commitments.
Define the safe semantic mapping and outcome/retry behavior. Add details only when needed, with explicit schema and size limits.
Verify the real transport envelope, status, code, safe message, correlation, hidden-resource handling, and relevant failure paths. Test absent/invalid/expired credentials and other lifecycle states only where that mechanism exists.
Inject unexpected failures and assert that secrets, SQL, provider data, input values, stacks, and internal paths do not escape. Verify one appropriate diagnostic event and safe retry metadata if present.
Regenerate and check the registry/OpenAPI/SDK references through [validation](../validation.md). Preserve current checks for registered unique codes, operation declarations, and freshness; extend checks for any new detail schemas or released compatibility obligations.
